greenhouse-year-1: A greenhouse is a device for managing sunlight. The glass lets the light in, and the same light heats the air, the soil and every surface inside. I built houses at Chatsworth before I built a palace, and in each I asked what jobs the parts did. A small house swings in temperature faster than a large one, because it has little air to soak up the swing, so it needs watching more closely, not less. As you read, list the sources of heat and the ways it escapes. Then write one sentence on what that means for how often you will look.

Pick the structure for a stated purpose, and site it before you buy it. The extension sources set out a ladder from the simplest cover to a full greenhouse, so ask how much cover your purpose needs. Orient the house to the light and the wind, and walk the plot at different times of day. Choose a covering by its trade-offs, not by its price. In my houses every part had more than one job, and I would have you ask the same of yours: what does this frame, this vent, this path do besides the obvious?

Air is the first and cheapest tool, and an undersized vent is the commonest cause of trouble. In the houses I described, the vents swung on pivots and opened by rods from one place, so the air could be adjusted. Work out how much opening you have for the size of your house, and ask whether you can reach it. Add circulation where air sits in layers, and watch moisture, since still damp air invites disease. Try opening vents earlier in the day and compare the log.

You cannot manage what you have not measured, and one thermometer in the wrong place will mislead you. Put sensors where the plants are, out of direct sun, and record at set times. Record the minimum and maximum, and humidity if you can. Read the pattern over several days before you act. At the Palace the readings were taken every two hours from many thermometers, and the habit is what matters: the same place, the same times, written down.
greenhouse-year-2: Think of the year as a harvest to be spread, not only a season to be survived. The sources start from a different premise from most gardeners: extend the harvest, not the growing season, and choose what survives the cold. I wrote that no single border is full all summer without contrivances, and the same is true of a house. As you read, list three crops that stand a cold spell and say where in the year each gives you something. The aim is a steady flow, not one arc.

Every calendar in this module hangs on two dates: the average last frost in spring and the first in autumn. Find them for your place from a local source, and use a range, not a single day. Work backwards from the harvest you want, counting the weeks each crop needs. Where the sources disagree, write both and say which you will test. I said what was true in my place, not everywhere, and you should do the same: mark the dates as yours.

A single sowing gives a glut and then a gap. Sow at intervals of one to three weeks, and pair quick crops with slow ones so that one finishes as the next fills the space. In my borders I planted oriental poppies beside gypsophila, so that the poppies finished as the gypsophila covered the ground. Draw the handover for one bed on a time line, with weeks, and check for gaps and for crowding.

Divide the year into four blocks, each with its own job for the house. Winter is for protecting, not forcing; spring for raising transplants; summer for heat-loving crops and keeping the rest cool; autumn for sowing what will stand the winter. Swap the blocks for your hemisphere. Give each block one purpose and a short list of crops. I gave each border its season, and it kept each one strong rather than half-dressed all year.
greenhouse-year-3: A seed needs the right temperature, moisture, humidity and light, and the medium may differ from the air by several degrees. I chose the pea because it met my conditions and tested it for two years before I used it. Do the same with your seed: check it against the conditions you can give. Make the environment ready before you sow, and write down what you provided. If a seed fails, the cause is more likely a missing condition than bad luck.

Clean containers and a good mix prevent trouble before it starts. The sources disagree on some choices, so set the options side by side and choose one for a stated reason. Fill the container evenly, level the surface and moisten the mix before you sow. Sanitise used trays. I protected my crosses from stray pollen, and a clean tray is the same kind of protection: it keeps out what you did not intend to introduce.

Sowing takes a minute; the first two weeks decide the result. Sow at the right depth and spacing, water without moving the seed, give warmth and cover as needed, and give light as soon as seedlings appear. Check the trays daily and count what you see. I counted every seed and reported the failures, and I would have you keep a log with the number sown, the number up and the number surviving. Watch for damping-off and write down the date you first see it.

A seedling in a tiny cell outgrows it before the bed is ready. Pot on at the right time, handle by the leaf and not the stem, thin the weak ones, and harden off gradually. Count again at each stage so you know the loss. Small trays fluctuate widely, as my plants did when I looked at them one at a time, so judge a seed lot by repeated trays. Record what you did and what you saw.
greenhouse-year-4: Poor growth often has a cause you can name. pH and EC tell you about the medium, and the alkalinity of your water tells you how fast the pH will drift. Learn what each number measures and why it matters. I looked for the missing constituent and then tested the fix. Make a list of the factors you can check before you blame anything else, and put the pH and EC in it. A reading is a clue, not a verdict.

Extract a sample of the medium solution with distilled water and measure the extract, rather than pushing a probe into the pot. The sources describe three methods: the PourThru, the saturated media extract and the 1:2 dilution. Read the EC result against the range for the method you used, because the ranges differ. Do one test the same way each time. When a result looks odd, repeat it before you act, and rule out the other causes before you fix the one you first suspected.

A single test tells you little. The value is in repeating it the same way and watching the trend. Keep your meter calibrated, test on a schedule, and record the date, the bench and the result in one place. Turn the column of numbers into a decision: what changed, what you will adjust, and what you will check next. When one thing is fixed, another may become the limit, so look for the next short stave.

How and when you water decides how much pH and EC move. Collect the guidance on supply, volume and timing into a routine you can log. Check the water you start with, since it can carry alkalinity that shifts the medium. Measure how much a crop uses over a week. Change one thing at a time on one bench and keep a control bench. Write down the result so that the next season starts from knowledge.
greenhouse-year-5: The temperature in a greenhouse is a balance of gains and losses. Sunlight brings energy in, heaters add more, and heat leaves through the covering, through gaps and to the night sky. Plants take a share by transpiring. Draw the balance for your house and mark the biggest gain and the biggest loss. I gave my glasshouse parts more than one job so that each helped manage the heat, and you should ask the same of yours.

Summer is when a greenhouse is most likely to harm its own crop. Use the ladder: choose cooler crops, then natural ventilation, then forced ventilation, then evaporative cooling, and shade last because it also cuts the light plants need. Ventilate first, and shade the outside of the glass, not the inside. At the Palace the vents worked from one position, the blades kept the rain out, and screens hung outside the glass. Write your own hot-day routine in four lines.

Winter asks how little heat you can use and still keep the crop healthy. Begin with crop choice, then add cover, then heat the air safely, then heat the roots if you must. Mix the air gently so that cold does not sit in the corners, and watch moisture. Write the rules for safe heating, and keep fuel and flame away from anything that burns. A plan that works at the coldest night is a plan you have tested before it arrives.

Manual ventilation depends on someone being at the door at the right moment, and in a small house that moment comes quickly. Decide what to automate, and set the trigger from your own log, not from a guess. A set point is a number you have earned by recording. I tested the houses I built and described what they did, and you should test a trigger the same way: set it, log it, and move it if the plants say so.
greenhouse-year-6: Integrated pest management uses cultural, biological, physical, mechanical and chemical tactics together, with scouting and records at the centre. Learn the six components and the four families of control. I asked, before reaching for the spray gun, whether any other method would do. Decide what damage you can tolerate before you start, and write it down. A pest on one leaf is information, and a pest on every plant is a decision.

The cheapest pest control is the pest that never arrives. Before a crop goes in, look at the whole house for places pests can hide, and clean them. Prevent problems through culture, with good spacing and clean water. Keep the house clean and the climate in the range the crop likes, not the pest. Write a short sanitation checklist and run it between crops. Prevention that you have logged is evidence for your review.

Scouting is the habit that makes everything else work. Use sticky cards, walk the same route, and check indicator plants. Record what you find, where and when. Early detection lets you use the gentlest response. Look also for the natural enemies, because I wanted to protect the controls built into the environment. Count the same plants at the same time each week, so the numbers can be compared.

Natural enemies can be bought and released, either a few early or many when the pest is established. Follow the guidelines for a biological programme, and wait for them to work before you judge. Use chemicals only if nothing else will do, sparingly and selectively, and in a way that does not destroy the biological control. Write a decision rule with numbers: at what count do you act, and with what. Review the result.
greenhouse-year-7: Every source you have read ends the same way: keep records. They answer three questions: what did I plan, what happened, and why. I kept my notes month by month, and the notes taught me more than my memory could. Look at what you have been recording already and find the gaps. Write for yourself a year from now, who will not remember what today felt like.

A good log is boring. It has the same columns every time, one row per event, a date on every row and the units written down. Use the five layouts in the lesson, and learn the few spreadsheet functions you need. Mark what is true only in your house, with the words 'in my experience in this place'. Decide how often each log is filled in, and put the schedule on the wall.

The end of a crop is the start of the next one. Record the harvest as it happens, clean out between crops, and reset the structure and the equipment at the turn of the season. Keep the notes short and exact. I wrote what I did and what I saw, and a line for next year. Do the same after each clean-out, so the next crop begins from a known state.

The annual review turns a year of records into a better plan. Follow the five steps: compare the plan with what happened, calculate the results, find the causes, decide the changes, and write them down. Mark which results are only true of your house. Compare with earlier years, because some things show only in the second or third year. Check your review against the five criteria, and be honest about what the data cannot say.
greenhouse-year-cap: A good capstone is small enough to finish and large enough to teach you something. Start from the fixed limits: your frost dates and the times you will be away. Choose a standard unit, a bed or a block of weeks, and repeat it. I drew a great building from repeated parts to a fixed deadline, after testing the parts on smaller houses. Test one unit first and then commit the year. Write down what you will actually run.

The capstone is marked against five criteria, and each needs evidence collected often enough to leave no gaps. Set up the logs and the checkpoints now. Decide how you will handle missing data honestly: say what is missing and why, and do not fill it in. A log with a gap you have explained is worth more than a tidy log you have invented. Put the checkpoints in your calendar.

At the end of the year you have logs, a calendar and a plan to compare with them. Assemble the deliverable, and check it against the five criteria before you mark it complete. Be plain about what worked and what did not. I would have you ask of each result whether it is a fact about your house or about all houses. Hand in what you can support.
